title: Grove Harvest
statement: A grove survey records the yield of every tree in a binary arrangement, given in level order (tree) with null for a missing child. A yield can be negative where a tree is diseased. A subtree is a node together with everything below it. A subtree is ordered when every yield in its left part is strictly smaller than its root's yield, every yield in its right part is strictly larger, and both parts are themselves ordered; a single node is ordered. Return the largest total yield over all ordered subtrees, or 0 when every ordered subtree has a negative total, because you may harvest nothing.
constraints: 1 <= tree.length <= 10000 (the number of serialized entries, counting null placeholders)
The first and last entries are not null, and a null node has no entries for children

examples.explanation: The whole tree is not ordered because 5 sits in the right part of 6 but is smaller than 6. The subtree rooted at 9 (9, 5, 12) is ordered with total 26, beating the subtree at 3 (3, 2, 4) with total 9.
The whole tree is ordered, but its total is -140 and every single node is negative, so the best harvest is nothing: 0.

hints.content: For every node ask two questions: is the subtree rooted here ordered, and what is its total?
Testing each node by walking its whole subtree works but repeats work on deep trees: O(n * height), up to O(n^2) on a chain.
If a subtree reports its smallest and largest yield, a parent can check the order rule in O(1): left.max < value < right.min.
So each node reports (ordered?, total, min, max) to its parent. A missing child reports ordered, total 0, min = +infinity and max = -infinity.

Compute these summaries in post-order, children before parents. A recursive function can return the summary, or, because level order lists every child after its parent, you can sweep node indexes from last to first and avoid deep recursion. Keep the largest total among ordered nodes, starting from 0.

testCases.explanation: A deeper subtree beats the broken whole tree.
A fully ordered tree whose yields are all negative gives 0.
The whole tree is a valid ordered tree.
Equal yields are not strictly ordered, so only single nodes count.
12 is fine under 5 but breaks the order of the root, so the subtree at 5 (total 18) is the best.
Mixed signs: the negative left child is never worth including.
A 5000-node increasing chain, the deepest tree the limit allows: the best subtree skips the negative front of the chain, and a recursive solution must survive 5,000 nested calls.
A large binary search tree with a dozen spoiled values.
A large random tree with many repeated yields.

solutions.title: Check every subtree with an in-order walk
solutions.intuition: A subtree is ordered exactly when its in-order walk is strictly increasing, so test each subtree on its own.
solutions.approach: Decode the level order into child index arrays. For each node, walk its subtree in order with an explicit stack, check that the yields strictly increase, and if so compare its total with the best.
solutions.pseudocode:
for root in nodes: walked = inorder(root)
  if walked strictly increasing: best = max(best, sum(walked))
solutions.timeComplexity: O(sum of all subtree sizes), which is O(n * height) and O(n^2) on a long chain
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the decoded arrays and the stack
commonMistakes: Allowing equal yields in the increasing check.
Checking only each node against its direct children, which misses a deeper descendant that breaks the order.
solutions.interviewExplanation: An in-order walk of a binary search tree is strictly increasing, so I test each subtree independently. It is easy to trust, but a degenerate tree makes the walks add up to O(n^2).

steps.title: Subtree at 9
steps.content: In-order walk is 5, 9, 12: strictly increasing, total 26.

steps.title: Whole tree
steps.content: In-order walk is 2, 3, 4, 6, 5, 9, 12: 6 followed by 5 breaks the order, so it does not count.

solutions.title: Iterative reverse sweep over the level order
solutions.intuition: Level order lists every parent before its children, so scanning node indexes from last to first is a post-order pass without any recursion.
solutions.approach: Decode the level order into child index arrays. Sweep node indexes from last to first so children are always finished before parents. For each node, require the left side to be ordered with max < value and the right side ordered with min > value; if so mark it ordered, add the totals and propagate min and max. Track the best total, starting at 0.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n) for n non-null nodes (the serialized length is at most 2n)
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the decoded child arrays and the per-node results; no recursion stack
commonMistakes: Sweeping from the first index to the last, which reads children before they have been summarised.
Starting best at -infinity, which returns a negative harvest when harvesting nothing is allowed.
Using the left child's value instead of its maximum as the bound for the parent.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This is the same (ordered, total, min, max) summary, computed iteratively. Because level order lists parents before children, a reverse index sweep visits children first, so no recursion is needed. That avoids a call stack as deep as the tree on degenerate inputs. Time is O(n); space is O(n) for the decoded arrays and the per-node results.

steps.title: Visit the leaves
steps.content: Leaves 2, 4, 5 and 12 return ordered summaries with low = high = their yield.

steps.title: Combine upward
steps.content: Node 9 accepts (5, 12) and returns total 26; node 6 rejects its right summary because low 5 is not above 6.

solutions.title: Recursive post-order returning (ordered, total, min, max)
solutions.intuition: The definition is recursive: a subtree is ordered when both child subtrees are ordered and their extremes straddle the root, so each call only needs to hand its parent four numbers.
solutions.approach: Decode the level order into child index arrays. visit(node) returns { ordered, total, low, high }: a missing child is ordered with total 0, low = +infinity and high = -infinity. A node is ordered when both children are, left.high < value and right.low > value; then its total is left.total + right.total + value, its low is min(left.low, value) and its high is max(right.high, value). Record the best total whenever a node is ordered, starting from 0.
solutions.pseudocode:
visit(n): if null: (true, 0, +inf, -inf)
  l = visit(n.left); r = visit(n.right)
  if not (l.ordered and r.ordered and l.high < n.v < r.low): return (false, ...)
  best = max(best, l.total + r.total + n.v); return (true, total, min(l.low, n.v), max(r.high, n.v))
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n) for n non-null nodes (the serialized length is at most 2n)
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the decoded child arrays, plus a recursion stack as deep as the tree is tall, which reaches O(n) on a chain
commonMistakes: Returning a summary for an unordered subtree whose low and high could still pass the parent's test; mark it unordered and never accept it.
Starting best at -infinity, which returns a negative harvest when harvesting nothing is allowed.
Comparing the node only with its direct children instead of the whole left maximum and right minimum.
Forgetting that a chain of thousands of nodes means thousands of nested calls; a reverse sweep over the level order avoids deep recursion.
solutions.interviewExplanation: A subtree is ordered when its left subtree is ordered with a maximum below the root, its right subtree is ordered with a minimum above the root, and the root lies strictly between them. So each subtree summarises itself as (ordered, total, min, max) and the parent combines two summaries in O(1). That is a natural post-order recursion and runs in O(n) time. The call stack is as deep as the tree is tall, so a degenerate tree of thousands of levels needs O(n) stack; the iterative reverse sweep trades the recursion for an index loop over the level order.

steps.title: Leaves first
steps.content: Nodes 2, 4, 5 and 12 are ordered singles with totals equal to their yields.

steps.title: Combine
steps.content: Node 9 has left max 5 < 9 and right min 12 > 9, total 26. Node 3 has total 9. Node 6 sees left max 4 < 6 but right min 5 < 6, so it is not ordered.

steps.title: Answer
steps.content: The best total among ordered nodes is 26.
